title: Lina and the Thirsty Bluebell
markdown:
The sun, a warm golden coin, peeked over the Whispering Woods and cast long sleepy shadows. A brook talked to itself. Lina, a gentle engineer with pockets that jingled useful bits — reeds, string, a pebble that was only sometimes useful — explored with Sunny the squirrel, whose bushy tail could shake acorns from high branches if he got too excited, which he often did. Dr. Sol walked beside them, beard white as dandelion fluff after a breeze, eyes twinkling like distant stars he did not mention.

“Look!” Sunny scampered ahead, paws barely disturbing the leaves. “Our bluebell friend is so droopy. Its pretty blue hat is floppy.”

A tiny bluebell, usually bright, petals like velvet cups, slumped. Stem bent like a tired dancer. Colour a little pale, as if it had forgotten how to smile. Lina knelt, careful as a butterfly landing. “It needs a drink.” She poured a little water from her canteen around the base. Instead of perking up, it wilted more, petals curling as if the water was too much, too fast. “Perhaps not thirsty after all?” Sunny’s whiskers quivered.

Lina examined more closely, engineer’s curiosity. She brushed soil with a finger: deep rich brown, cool earth. The poured water sat lonely, a puddle on a path. The roots were tiny thin white straws, buried. The stem a little green pipe, strong but slender. Quiet wonder, like watching a seed sprout. “The water just sits on top. It can’t get in. It doesn’t drink from the top, like pouring on a leaf. It drinks from its feet. Roots like tiny mouths, pulling water up the stem — a clever tube.”

The idea bubbled like fizzy lemonade. She rummaged: a smooth hollow reed she had found by the babbling brook that morning, soft fluffy moss from a log that smelled of rain. Clever hands fashioned a funnel from a large sturdy leaf, pinched and tucked, attached to one end of the reed. She tested it with a drop on her palm first — yes, it ran through. Then she pushed the other end into the soil near the roots, snug, not so deep as to poke the white straws. Moss nestled around it, a tiny soft bed for the pipe. “Now the water can go straight to the roots. A gentle stream to a thirsty mouth. Not a puddle sitting on top, looking lonely.”

They watched, holding their breath. The forest seemed to as well. A bird started a song and then thought better of interrupting. Slowly the water trickled down the reed — Lina counted three drops she could see — and seeped around the roots. Silent, patient. Nothing, for a long blink. Then the stem began to straighten, one shy inch. Petals lifted toward the sun, colour returning, bright as sky, the floppy hat remembering how to be a cup. A soft rustle through the leaves. Sunny clapped without meaning to, and an acorn fell, which he pretended he had planned.

Sol smiled, eyes crinkling like rings on an old tree. Roots like little pumps, stem a tiny pipe, nourishment to the flower. How plants stay fresh on dry days. He left the wisdom-and-kindness speech short.

Sunny bounced. “It drinks with its roots, like I drink with my mouth!”

Lina beamed at the cheerful bluebell, tall again. She did not wonder what other secrets plants hid, or wait for the flower to nod thank you. She left the reed in place, moss tucked, so the next dry afternoon would not become another puddle on the path. Sunny pretended to sip from a dewdrop, which was showing off, and Lina let him.
